newsitem.title: INDIA: Cement prices slip in southern India, demand rises.
newsitem.headline: Cement prices slip in southern India, demand rises.

text.p: Cement prices have started softening in the southern state of Kerala following the entry of Bombay-based Larsen & Toubro Ltd (L&T) in this market, some manufacturers and analysts said on Tuesday.

However, demand for cement in southern markets had spurted after the 1997/98 (April-March) budget unveiled on February 28, a senior official of India Cements, a leading player in southern India, said.
Cement prices in south India are traditionally the highest in the country because there are few producers in the region.
Growth in Indian cement demand fell to less than 10 percent in the second half of 1996/97 (April-March) from over 12 percent in the first half, largely reflecting a slowdown in the economy.

Vice president (marketing) of another cement firm operating from the Tamil Nadu state adjoining Kerala, who did not want to be identified, said cement prices have fallen by two to three rupees per 50 kg bag to about 172 rupees in Kerala.

L&T began shipping cement to Kerala coast from its plant on the western Gujarat coast early this year. L&T plans to increase shipments after it commissions its cement terminal on the western coast, now in advanced stage of completion.
"Prices in Kerala are down by a couple of rupees per bag," said Ajay Malpani, cement analyst at Caspian Research in Bombay.
But an official of India Cements Ltd, a leading player in the region, denied that L&T's entry had hurt prices.
"L&T was always present in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, supplying by rail," T.V. Swaminathan, India Cements' general manager (operations) told Reuters over the phone from Madras.
L&T's supplies to Kerala were less than 20,000 tonnes a month against the state's monthly demand of 300,000 tonnes.
"There is a general slackness in Kerala but we are not under any pressure," Swaminathan said.
"There is a boom in demand ever since the budget," he said.
"It is too early to say there's an uptrend in demand," Caspian's Malpani said. "January to May is usually a strong period for cement."

India Cements' Swaminathan said prices continued to be firm in Tamil Nadu. He said his firm's cement prices were stable at 160-165 rupees per 50 kg bag in Madras city and 177-180 rupees elsewhere in the state.
Bombay-based securities firm First Global Finance said new capacities coming on stream from Madras Cements and India Cements later this month may put pressure on prices.
"Price realisation in Kerala have come down by five to six rupees per bag as supplies from L&T and Saurashtra Cements have started hitting the market," First Global said in a report.
Another dampener could be a possible hike in the power tariff in Tamil Nadu, it said. The power tariff in Tamil Nadu have not been raised for almost two years, it added.
"Overall, pressure on realisations and margins is expected to continue for the next year or so, unless informal caterlisation takes place," it concluded.
India is the world's fourth largest cement producer.
